words.definition: to accept or agree to something without protest
words.origin: Latin acquiescere, to rest or remain quiet
words.mnemonic: A C before the Q, and an S-C near the end: ac-qui-esce.
sentences: After a long debate, the board chose to acquiesce to the new plan.
She would not acquiesce just because everyone else agreed.

words.definition: to make something bad or unsatisfactory better
words.mnemonic: Hide the Latin melior (better) inside: a-melior-ate.
sentences: New bike lanes helped ameliorate traffic downtown.
Nothing could ameliorate the sting of losing in the final round.

words.definition: something that belongs to a different time period
words.origin: Greek ana, against, and khronos, time
words.mnemonic: Chronos is time, spelled with CH, as in chronological.
sentences: A wristwatch on a Roman soldier is an obvious anachronism.
The fax machine in the office felt like an anachronism.

words.definition: hostile and eager to fight or argue
words.mnemonic: Bellum (war) brings the double L.
sentences: The belligerent customer shouted at every employee.
His tone turned belligerent as soon as he lost the argument.

words.definition: changing mood or behavior suddenly and without reason
words.mnemonic: Like delicious, it ends in -cious.
sentences: Spring weather here is capricious, so pack an umbrella.
The capricious manager changed the deadline three times.

words.definition: an expert judge in matters of taste, such as food or art
words.mnemonic: Double N, double S, and a French -eur ending.
sentences: A true connoisseur can name the coffee bean by taste alone.
He became a connoisseur of street food while traveling.

words.definition: careful to do one's work or duty well
words.mnemonic: Science is hiding inside: con-SCIEN-tious.
sentences: A conscientious student double-checks every answer.
She is conscientious about replying to every email.

words.definition: a person who dabbles in a subject without real commitment
words.mnemonic: One L, then a double T: dil-et-tante.
sentences: He is a dilettante who starts a new hobby every month.
Critics dismissed her as a dilettante, but her paintings sold out.

words.definition: shockingly bad
words.origin: Latin egregius, standing out from the flock
words.mnemonic: E-GREG-ious: Greg stood out from the flock, for the wrong reasons.
sentences: Charging twenty dollars for water is an egregious markup.
The referee made an egregious call in the final minute.

words.definition: a habit or way of behaving that is peculiar to one person
words.origin: Greek idios, own, and synkrasis, mixture
words.mnemonic: It ends in -crasy, not -cracy like democracy.
sentences: Humming while she reads is her strangest idiosyncrasy.
Every old house has some idiosyncrasy, like a door that sticks.

words.definition: sweet and smooth to hear
words.origin: Latin mel, honey, and fluere, to flow
words.mnemonic: Honey (mel) that flows (flu): mel-li-flu-ous.
sentences: The narrator's mellifluous voice made the audiobook a joy.
A mellifluous melody drifted out of the cafe.

words.definition: done secretly because it would not be approved of
words.mnemonic: Double R, then a single P sneaks in quietly.
sentences: He took a surreptitious glance at his phone during the meeting.
Their surreptitious snack run went unnoticed.

words.definition: not indulging much in food or drink
words.origin: Latin abstemius, from abs-, away from, and temetum, strong drink
words.mnemonic: It has all five vowels in order: a, e, i, o, u.
sentences: Their abstemious grandfather never had more than one coffee a day.
An abstemious diet before the race left him hungry but fast.

words.definition: showing great care and steady effort
words.origin: Latin assiduus, sitting down to a task
words.mnemonic: Double S as you sit down to work: as-sid-u-ous.
sentences: An assiduous editor caught every missing comma.
Her assiduous practice paid off at the recital.

words.definition: trust and friendship among people who spend time together
words.mnemonic: Three A's in a row of syllables, then -derie: ca-ma-ra-de-rie.
sentences: The team's camaraderie carried them through a losing season.
Long night shifts built a strong camaraderie among the nurses.

words.definition: to remove the moisture from something
words.mnemonic: One S, two C's, the opposite of what most people guess.
sentences: The desert wind will desiccate any fruit left outside.
Chefs desiccate coconut to make it last for months.

words.definition: cheerful and full of energy
words.mnemonic: Energy boils over, and so do the L's: e-bul-lient.
sentences: Her ebullient laugh filled the whole room.
The coach was ebullient after the upset win.

words.definition: very attentive to detail and hard to please
words.mnemonic: A fastidious person is fast to tidy: fas-tid-ious.
sentences: He is fastidious about keeping his desk clear.
A fastidious baker weighs flour to the gram.

words.definition: a long, loud and aggressive speech
words.origin: Old French arenge, a speech to a crowd
words.mnemonic: It ends in -ngue, like tongue: you harangue with your tongue.
sentences: The manager delivered a ten-minute harangue about being late.
Nobody wanted to sit through another harangue at dinner.

words.definition: casually unconcerned
words.mnemonic: No souci (French for worry) inside: in-SOUCI-ant.
sentences: He gave an insouciant shrug when the bus pulled away without him.
Her insouciant attitude hid how hard she had studied.

words.definition: noisy and difficult to control
words.origin: Latin obstrepere, to make a noise against
words.mnemonic: Strep throat from all that shouting: ob-STREP-erous.
sentences: The obstreperous crowd chanted through the entire speech.
An obstreperous toddler can empty a quiet cafe.

words.definition: quick to notice and understand things
words.mnemonic: Per-spi-ca-cious: only one C until the -cious ending, like delicious.
sentences: A perspicacious reader spotted the twist by chapter two.
Her perspicacious questions exposed the flaw in the plan.

words.definition: stubbornly refusing to obey or cooperate
words.origin: Latin recalcitrare, to kick back with the heels
words.mnemonic: It kicks back with C then C: re-Cal-Ci-trant.
sentences: The recalcitrant printer jammed on every page.
Even the most recalcitrant student joined the debate.

words.definition: treating something sacred with disrespect
words.origin: Latin sacrilegus, a stealer of sacred things
words.mnemonic: Not religious: the I and E swap places, sac-RI-LE-gious.
sentences: Putting pineapple on that pizza felt sacrilegious to the chef.
Talking during the film was sacrilegious to my sister.

words.definition: an unwelcome change in circumstances
words.mnemonic: One C, then a double S: vi-cis-si-tude.
sentences: Every startup faces some vicissitude in its first year.
She handled each vicissitude of the long trip with humor.
